title: EAV, JSON column, wide table or document?

rows.label: In one line
values: One row per fact: entity, attribute, value
Known fields as columns, the rest in one JSON column
One column per attribute, mostly NULL
Each record is a self-contained JSON-like document

rows.label: Adding an attribute
values: Insert a row into the attribute catalog; no DDL
Just write the new key; no DDL
`ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN`; in PostgreSQL a nullable column is a metadata change, with no table rewrite
Just write the new field; no DDL

rows.label: Types
values: Typed value columns or one value table per type, chosen from metadata; often everything ends up as text
JSON’s string, number, boolean and null; dates are strings until you cast them
Any SQL type, per column
BSON types in MongoDB, including dates, 64-bit integers and Decimal128

rows.label: Constraints
values: None per attribute in the schema; enforced by triggers that read metadata, or by the application
`CHECK` constraints on expressions; JSON Schema via MySQL’s `JSON_SCHEMA_VALID` or PostgreSQL extensions
Ordinary `NOT NULL`, `CHECK` and foreign keys on each column
Optional `$jsonSchema` validation per collection; no foreign keys

rows.label: Indexing
values: `(attribute, value)` indexes, one attribute at a time; multi-attribute filters become joins
GIN over the whole column, expression indexes per key, or generated columns; MySQL indexes only generated columns and arrays
A B-tree per column you filter on; SQL Server adds filtered indexes on sparse columns
Any field, including nested fields and arrays (multikey indexes)

rows.label: Query shape
values: Pivot with one `CASE` or join per attribute
Operators and casts: `props->>'plan'`, `props @> '{...}'`, JSON path
Plain `SELECT col WHERE col = ...`
Field paths in find and aggregation; `$lookup` for joins between collections

rows.label: Planner statistics
values: Per column, so all attributes share one histogram
None on keys inside the column unless you add an expression index or `CREATE STATISTICS`
Per column, as for any table
MongoDB races candidate index plans in a short trial; a cost-based ranker covers some queries since 8.3

rows.label: Sparse data on disk
values: Only present facts, but each is a full row with IDs and a row header (about 23 bytes in PostgreSQL)
Only present keys, but every row repeats its key names
A NULL costs one bit in PostgreSQL’s null bitmap; SQL Server sparse columns shrink NULLs at extra cost per non-NULL value
Only present fields, but every document repeats its field names (BSON stores each name)

rows.label: Limits
values: Practically unlimited attributes
Large documents work, but any update locks the whole row; keep them small
1,600 columns per table in PostgreSQL; 1,024 in SQL Server, or 30,000 with sparse column sets
16 MiB per document in MongoDB

rows.label: Reporting and BI
values: Pivot first, into views, materialized views or exports
Tools see one opaque column; extract keys into views or columns
Works directly
Usually flattened into a warehouse first

rows.label: Pick it when
values: Attributes are user-defined data with thousands of possibilities and a handful per entity
A relational app has a varying tail of fields you don’t yet understand
Attributes are known, at most a few hundred, and you report on them
Whole records vary and are read and written as one unit

rows.label: Seen in
values: WordPress meta tables, Magento catalog, clinical data repositories, RDF triple stores
PostgreSQL `jsonb`, MySQL `JSON`, SQLite JSON functions, Snowflake VARIANT
Survey and feature tables, SQL Server sparse columns
MongoDB, Firestore, Cosmos DB, DocumentDB

tip: Start with columns for every field you know you’ll query, and put the unpredictable rest in a JSON column. Watch which keys get used and promote those to real or generated columns. Reach for EAV only when attributes are themselves data that users define, and you’re ready to build the metadata layer it needs; switch to a document database when whole records, not just a tail of fields, vary.
